summary.text: Specializing the “moreover” claim to \(n=7\), the prescribed choices force \(x\ge 3\); since \(x\le y\le z\), this gives \(x+y+z\ge 9\), contradicting \(x+y+z=7\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]
The conjecture asserts a conjunction. Its first clause says that for every integer \(n>5\), the number \(a(n)\) of admissible ordered triples is positive. Its second, stronger (“moreover”) clause says that for every integer \(n>6\), there exist positive integers \(x,y,z\) such that
\[
x+y+z=n,\qquad x\le y\le z,\qquad x\in S,
\]
and such that all six numbers
\[
2x-1,\quad 2y-1,\quad 2z-1,\quad 2xy-1,\quad 2xz-1,\quad 2yz-1
\]
are prime.

We disprove the second clause by taking \(n=7\). Certainly \(7>6\), so if the conjecture were true, there would be positive integers \(x,y,z\) satisfying all the conditions above with
\[
x+y+z=7.
\]

Because \(x\in S\), there are five possibilities:
\[
x=3,\quad x=4,\quad x=6,\quad x=10,\quad\text{or}\quad x=15.
\]
In every case, \(x\ge 3\). The ordering conditions now give
\[
y\ge x\ge 3
\quad\text{and}\quad
z\ge y\ge x\ge 3.
\]
Consequently,
\[
x+y+z\ge 3+3+3=9.
\]
This contradicts the required equality \(x+y+z=7\).

Thus no triple can satisfy even the elementary membership, ordering, and sum conditions for \(n=7\); in particular, no triple can satisfy those conditions together with the six primality requirements. Hence the universal “moreover” clause is false. Since that clause is one conjunct of the stated conjecture, the whole conjecture is false, independently of whether its first clause \(a(n)>0\) might hold.
